cases.title: Arequipa uprising over Egasa and Egesur sale
cases.point: Plaza Mayor, central Arequipa, where a student was hit by a tear-gas canister (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Peru's January 2002 letter of intent to the IMF listed 'Privatization of the electricity generation company Egasa' as a structural benchmark due by 30 September 2002, and set asset-sale proceeds of at least US$700 million a year.

cases.conditions: IMF letter of intent, 18 January 2002: privatizations to 'focus in the energy sector'; structural benchmarks for selling Etecen and Jorbsa (by June 2002) and Egasa (by September 2002). Egesur is not named in the letter. In November 2002 Peru told the IMF that the sale of two public firms, both program benchmarks, had been held up, and asked to change the privatization targets.

companies.name: Tractebel (Suez group)
companies.role: Sole bidder; agreed on 14 June 2002 to buy Egasa and Egesur for US$167 million

cases.community: The sale went against a campaign promise by President Toledo not to sell the two firms. Arequipa rose up with marches, strikes and road blocks; the mayor went on hunger strike. Página/12 reported dozens injured on the first day of clashes; News & Letters reported several hundred injured. Two young men died, one of them a university student hit in the head by a police tear-gas canister. Strikes spread to Tacna, Cuzco, Puno and Moquegua; in Tacna several hundred people were arrested.
cases.suppression: On 16 June 2002 the government declared a state of emergency and curfew in Arequipa and Tacna and sent in the armed forces. Police used tear gas against crowds.
cases.killed_note: Página/12 (20 June 2002) names Edgar Pinto, 30, and student Fernando Talavera; News & Letters also counts two dead.
cases.outcome: On 19 June 2002 the government agreed with Arequipa's mayors to suspend the sale until a court ruled, lifted the state of emergency and issued a public apology. The two firms were not sold to Tractebel. Peru's November 2002 letter to the IMF cut expected privatization receipts for 2002 to US$400 million.

cases.title: TANESCO management contract with NETGroup
cases.point: Dar es Salaam, seat of the state power utility TANESCO (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Made power-sector reform a lending condition in 1993. The contract was paid through a World Bank trust fund (money from Sweden's Sida), and the Bank had to approve each stage (Ghanadan and Eberhard 2007).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Tanzania's August 2001 letter of intent to the IMF said the government had decided to hire a management company to run TANESCO from November 2001, and to let TANESCO raise average tariffs. The July 2003 letter listed TANESCO among utilities still to be privatized.

cases.conditions: IMF letter of intent, 31 August 2001: engage a management company for TANESCO and raise the average electricity tariff. IMF letter of intent, 10 July 2003: medium-term focus on privatizing large utilities including TANESCO. World Bank: sector reform a lending condition since 1993 (Ghanadan and Eberhard).

companies.name: NETGroup Solutions
companies.role: Managed TANESCO from May 2002 to December 2006; paid about US$18–19 million, mostly tied to revenue collection
companies.hq: South Africa (city not given in sources)

cases.community: In 2003 more than 1,280 workers (about 21% of staff) were retrenched; staff fell from 6,540 (2002) to 4,787 (2005). Residential tariffs rose about 39% from 2001 to 2006 while large industrial tariffs fell 22–28%. Bills for homes using over 50 kWh a month nearly tripled from 2000 to 2005 while prices overall rose about 25%. The low-use 'lifeline' block was cut from 100 to 50 kWh. About 15,000–20,000 customers were cut off each month; from May 2002 to June 2005 there were 713,720 disconnections against 569,770 customers. Load shedding reached 12–16 hours a day in 2006. All figures: Ghanadan and Eberhard (2007).
cases.suppression: The government refused a parliamentary request to make the contract public (SADOCC news, 2002).
cases.outcome: Revenue collection nearly doubled, but losses and reliability did not improve and new connections fell short of targets (Ghanadan and Eberhard). The contract ended in December 2006; TANESCO was not sold.

cases.title: SONEL electricity sale to AES
cases.point: Douala, Cameroon's main city and seat of AES-SONEL (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The third Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC III, 1998–2004, US$180 million) listed completing privatization of public utilities as a key goal. Pineau (2004) calls the sale a commitment to meet one of SAC III's requirements.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Cameroon's December 2001 letter of intent reported to the IMF that SONEL's privatization had been completed, alongside pending sales of the water company SNEC and telecoms firm CAMTEL.

cases.conditions: World Bank SAC III: complete the privatization program, especially public utilities (Pineau 2004). IMF letter of intent, 28 December 2001, reports SONEL privatization as done.

companies.name: AES Corporation
companies.role: Sole bidder; bought 56% of SONEL in July 2001; contract never published

companies.name: Actis
companies.role: Bought AES's 56% stake for US$220 million in 2013–14; company renamed ENEO

cases.community: The concession set tariff rises above inflation of 5% (2001) and 7.5% a year (2002–2004). The low-voltage 'social' block was cut from 110 kWh a month to 50 kWh in 2004. Medium-voltage fixed charges jumped from 9.125 FCFA per kW a year to 2,500–4,000 FCFA per kW a month. The aluminium smelter ALUCAM kept paying 5 FCFA/kWh. Blackouts became much more frequent; a French Development Agency estimate cited by Pineau puts the growth loss at about 1%. A lawyer reported at least 57 court cases seeking compensation for outage losses. About 360 workers took early retirement.
cases.outcome: Load shedding continued into the 2020s (Journal du Cameroun, cited on Wikipedia). A 2011 law moved transmission back to a state firm, SONATREL, which began work in 2018.

cases.title: Mozambique bank sales (BCM and Banco Austral)
cases.point: Banco Austral headquarters, Avenida 25 de Setembro, Maputo (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The IMF listed the 1996 privatization of the Commercial Bank of Mozambique (BCM) among the reforms under its ESAF loan. Joseph Hanlon reports the IMF said aid would stop if the People's Development Bank (BPD) was not privatized by 30 June 1997.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: With the IMF, recommended a second sale of Banco Austral in 2001 to avoid liquidation (Mail & Guardian).

cases.conditions: IMF press release, 24 June 1997 (second annual ESAF loan): BCM privatized in 1996; privatization program to be completed by mid-1999. BPD sale deadline of 30 June 1997 under threat of aid cuts (Hanlon, Club of Mozambique, 2024).

companies.name: Southern Bank Berhad
companies.role: Led the Malaysian–Mozambican consortium (with Frelimo-linked Invester) that bought BPD in 1997 and renamed it Banco Austral

companies.name: ABSA
companies.role: Bought 80% of Banco Austral in the 2001 re-sale

cases.community: About US$14 million vanished from BCM before its 1996 sale. Journalist Carlos Cardoso, who was investigating that fraud, was shot dead in Maputo on 22 November 2000. At Banco Austral, the new owners piled up more than US$200 million in bad loans (Mail & Guardian); a KPMG audit found management had looted over US$40 million in three years (Hanlon). The state took the bank back in April 2001. Central-bank official António Siba-Siba Macuácua, put in charge of cleaning it up, was thrown down the stairwell of its headquarters on 11 August 2001, a day before he was due to give ABSA the bank's figures.
cases.suppression: The Siba-Siba case was dismissed in 2009; three men were only charged in September 2024. Hanlon reports donors raised aid at the October 2001 meeting despite the unsolved killings.
cases.killed_note: Carlos Cardoso (22 Nov 2000) and António Siba-Siba Macuácua (11 Aug 2001), per Wikipedia, Mail & Guardian and Hanlon.
cases.outcome: ABSA took 80% of Banco Austral for about US$10–15 million in late 2001. Aníbal dos Santos was sentenced to 30 years for organizing Cardoso's murder.

sources.title: Press Release 97/28: IMF Approves Second Annual ESAF Loan for Mozambique

cases.confidence_note: The IMF's own text confirms BCM's sale was part of its program; the BPD deadline and aid threat come from Hanlon's reporting, not an IMF document. The BCM fraud took place before the sale. Who ordered the killings is not settled in court.

cases.title: Argentine railway privatisation
cases.point: Once station, Buenos Aires, hub of the national rail network (approximate stand-in for a country-wide case)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Signed a 1990 restructuring program with the state railway (FA) and the ministry, the first official document to propose taking FA out of passenger service (Wikipedia). IPS reports the Bank recommended privatization and lent US$800 million to pay severance to 80,000 public workers who lost their jobs.

cases.conditions: 1990 FA–Ministry–World Bank restructuring program: private concessionaires only on freight lines; intercity passenger services (except Buenos Aires–Mar del Plata) to end on 1 January 1993 unless provinces took them over. World Bank severance loan of US$800 million (IPS).

companies.name: Trenes de Buenos Aires (TBA)
companies.role: Commuter concession on the Mitre and Sarmiento lines; revoked May 2012

companies.name: Metropolitano
companies.role: Commuter concessions; San Martín line revoked 2004, two more in 2007

cases.community: Rail jobs fell from 95,000 to 15,000; closures of rail-supply firms cost another 20,000 jobs (IPS, citing engineer Elido Veschi). The network shrank from 35,000 km to 8,500 km. Several interior cities lost their train to the capital and some villages became ghost towns. By 2002 subsidies to concessionaires cost about US$400 million a year, roughly what the state had spent running the network. A 2003 regulator report found 70% of inspected cars had faults such as brakes. By late 2003, 389 commuter passengers had died in accidents (IPS).
cases.killed_note: IPS counts 389 commuter deaths in accidents by late 2003, and the 2012 Once crash killed 51 (BBC via Wikipedia), but no source cited here ties a specific death toll to the World Bank-backed program, so no figure is entered.
cases.outcome: On 22 February 2012 a TBA train crashed at Once station, killing 51 and injuring over 700; TBA's concession was revoked in May 2012. In 2015 Congress passed a law returning the railways to the state (Nuevos Ferrocarriles Argentinos).

sources.title: Railway privatisation in Argentina
Argentina: rail privatisation derails (IPS report, 2004)

cases.confidence_note: The World Bank's restructuring document cited by Wikipedia could not be opened; the Bank's role rests on Wikipedia and IPS. The privatisation law (Law 23,696, 1989) was Argentina's own.

cases.title: Karachi Electric (KESC) sale and 2011 mass sacking

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Pakistan's November 2001 letter of intent to the IMF committed to bring KESC 'to the point of sale by July 2002' through a public offer, and to raise power tariffs toward cost.

cases.conditions: IMF letter of intent and memorandum of economic and financial policies, 22 November 2001: cabinet to approve a KESC privatization strategy by end-2001 and bring it to the point of sale by July 2002; electricity and gas tariffs to move toward cost.

companies.name: KES Power consortium (KES Power, Hasan Associates, Premier Mercantile)
companies.role: Bought 73% of KESC in November 2005 for Rs 15.86 billion (Rs 1.65 a share, while shares traded above Rs 7)

companies.name: Abraaj Capital
companies.role: Later took over the shares

cases.community: In January 2011 KESC sacked 4,500 workers (Dawn); the ITUC counts 4,300. Workers held a sit-in, and protests shut parts of the city's network. A critic quoted in Newsline says line losses rose from 34.2% to 40% after the sale, with long daily outages.
cases.suppression: KESC filed police complaints (FIRs) against striking workers (Dawn).
cases.outcome: After a government committee stepped in, KESC withdrew the sackings on 23 January 2011 and reinstated the workers.

cases.title: Nicaragua power distribution sale to Unión Fenosa
cases.point: Managua, where protesters marched against Unión Fenosa (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Nicaragua's 1999 ESAF Policy Framework Paper says ENEL was split in May 1999 'in preparation for privatization' and its generation and distribution units would be offered for sale by December 1999.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Co-author of the Policy Framework Paper process; Specht (2015) says Fenosa's contract was underwritten by World Bank guarantees.

cases.conditions: IMF/World Bank ESAF Policy Framework Paper, 1999: ENEL generation and distribution units to be offered for sale by December 1999; 40% of telecoms firm ENITEL to be tendered in January 2000; water systems in several cities offered for private management.

companies.name: Unión Fenosa
companies.role: Sole bidder; bought the distribution companies for about US$115 million, slightly over half the government's valuation (Specht); main distributor from 2000

cases.community: Power cuts grew to up to 10 hours a day (Specht) and, during the 2006 drought, rationing reached 15 hours a day (IPS). About half the population had grid power and the network barely grew under Fenosa; about 30% of power was lost before reaching paying users (Specht). Fenosa sought higher prices and added charges; prices became the highest in Central America (Specht).
cases.outcome: In August 2006 thousands marched in Managua demanding Fenosa's removal, and in Masaya protesters stoned its offices (IPS). President Ortega later called the company 'a mafia' (El Nuevo Diario, cited by Specht).

cases.title: Senelec power privatisation and union jailings
cases.point: Dakar, seat of Senelec and of the court that tried the union leaders (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Senegal's ESAF Policy Framework Paper 1998–2000 set dates: launch bids for Senelec's privatization in August 1998, hand it to a strategic partner by end-1998, and cut state ownership to no more than 41% before April 1999.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Co-author of the Policy Framework Paper with the government and IMF.

cases.conditions: ESAF Policy Framework Paper 1998–2000 (IMF/World Bank): law restructuring the power sector (April 1998); bids for Senelec (August 1998); strategic partner (end-1998); state share at most 41% (before April 1999).

companies.name: Hydro-Québec International
companies.role: With Elyo, bought 34% of Senelec in March 1999 (about US$66 million, PSIRU)

companies.name: Elyo (Suez Lyonnaise des Eaux)
companies.role: Consortium partner

cases.community: Power workers struck against the planned sale; the strike left much of Senegal without electricity. After the sale the new partners did not make the promised investment, and shortages followed; Social Watch names the shortage as the main cause of slower growth in 2002.
cases.suppression: On 20 July 1998 police arrested union leader Mademba Sock and 25 SUTELEC delegates at dawn, holding them four days without lawyers or family (complaint to the African Commission). On 8 December 1998 a Dakar court sentenced Sock to six months for acts likely to 'compromise public security'; he was freed on 23 January 1999.
cases.outcome: President Abdoulaye Wade annulled the sale in March 2000 and the consortium left in January 2001. A second attempt to sell 51% failed when the buyer, Vivendi, could not meet its commitments (Social Watch).

cases.title: Luanshya mines sale to Binani (RAMCOZ)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Fraser and Lungu (2007) list repeated Bank loan conditions to privatize the state copper firm ZCCM: PIRC II (1993), ERIP (1995), ESAC II (1996) and a 1999 credit.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: ESAF loans (1995, 1999) also required ZCCM privatization plans; HIPC debt relief depended on IMF and Bank reviews (Fraser and Lungu).

cases.conditions: World Bank PIRC II (1993): study options to privatize ZCCM; ERIP and IMF ESAF (1995), ESAC II (1996), and 1999 Bank and IMF loans: carry out ZCCM privatization (Fraser and Lungu 2007, For Whom the Windfalls?).

companies.name: Binani Group
companies.role: Bought 85% of Roan Antelope Mining Corporation of Zambia (RAMCOZ: Luanshya and Baluba mines) in 1997

cases.community: Binani soon abandoned the investment. By November 2000 the state bank ZANACO moved to put RAMCOZ in receivership, 5,000 jobs were at risk, and the power company cut supply over nearly US$10 million in unpaid bills (IRIN). Miners held a sit-in to demand money owed. The mines then sat idle for three years (Fraser and Lungu). Across ZCCM, jobs fell from about 31,000 at sale to 19,145 in 2001.
cases.suppression: Paramilitary police were sent to the plant to head off demonstrations when the receivership was announced (IRIN, November 2000).
cases.outcome: In 2004 a Swiss investor (J&W, a subsidiary of Enya) bought the assets, now Luanshya Mines Plc (Fraser and Lungu).

cases.title: Orissa power reform and distribution sale

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Set aside US$350 million for Orissa's power sector, paid in tranches tied to restructuring milestones (Prayas Energy Group, 2001).

cases.conditions: World Bank Orissa power sector restructuring loan (US$350 million, tranches tied to milestones): unbundle the state electricity board (1996), set up a regulator, and sell 51% of four distribution companies (done 1999). The Bank's appraisal assumed retail tariff rises of 15% and 18% in the first two years.

companies.name: AES Transpower
companies.role: Took over CESCO, the central zone distribution company, in 1999

companies.name: BSES
companies.role: Took over the other three distribution companies in 1999

cases.community: Average retail tariffs rose about 11% (1997), 9.3% (1998) and 4.5% (2000). Distribution losses stayed above 40% in all four companies. The state transmission firm GRIDCO's power purchase bill rose from Rs 150 crore (1996) to Rs 1,200 crore (2000) and it became technically bankrupt. Prayas warned that cost-based tariffs would hit rural and farm users hardest.
cases.outcome: The regulator approved a restructuring plan in March 2001 and criticised the original financial model (Prayas).

lenders.role: In March 1999 agreed to guarantee the AES Bujagali dam against political risk on condition that Uganda privatize the Uganda Electricity Board; a Bank document called a private sector 'crucial to the sustainability of the project' (Bayliss and Hall, PSIRU). The Bank's 1993 agreement also required tariff rises of about 5% a year in dollar terms (Eberhard chapter).

cases.conditions: World Bank guarantee for Bujagali (1999), conditional on privatizing the Uganda Electricity Board (PSIRU, 2000). 1993 Bank agreement: tariff rises of about 5% a year in US dollar terms.

companies.role: 20-year distribution concession from 2005

companies.name: Globeleq
companies.role: Majority owner of Umeme at launch

companies.role: Minority owner of Umeme at launch

cases.community: Average tariffs rose about 37.5% in June 2006 and another 41% in November 2006, to about US 17.2 cents per kWh. cases.title: Gécamines voluntary departure program
cases.point: Likasi, where the ex-workers who complained to the Inspection Panel live (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The Private Sector Development and Competitiveness credit (US$120 million, 2003) and a US$25 million tranche of the Economic Recovery Credit paid for severance of 10,655 Gécamines workers (World Bank management response). Ex-workers told the Inspection Panel the Bank made its funding depend on large staff cuts.

cases.conditions: PSDC Project (IDA Credit 3815-DRC), Component 2, parastatal reform: finance severance to shrink Gécamines' workforce (about 11,200 eligible). The project document calls the cuts government policy.

companies.name: Gécamines
companies.role: State mining company that cut its workforce

cases.community: 10,655 workers left between August 2003 and February 2004, with average pay-outs of US$4,083 (Bank figures). The ex-workers say wage arrears, final settlements, housing and other benefits went unpaid, and that they were forced into poverty. A 2006 evaluation found most started some income activity, but only about 100 small firms were launched and 230 of 1,200 hectares set aside were farmed.
cases.suppression: Ex-workers' letters to the Bank in early 2009 went unanswered; Bank management admitted it 'did not respond to all the emails'.
cases.outcome: In August 2011 the Inspection Panel chose not to investigate after management promised an action plan (school fees, health care, pension access, about US$12–14 million re-allocated). The Panel said the Bank's handling of risks 'could have been better'.
